scams.name: Rental Car Smash-and-Grab
scams.tldr: Your bags are in the trunk — it's a trunk, it's locked, you're not worried.
scams.description:
Your bags are in the trunk — it's a trunk, it's locked, you're not worried. You come back to a smashed window, glass on the seat, and everything gone. Welcome to San Francisco's most reliable tourist tax.

Travelers have documented this epidemic for years with near-clinical detail. The warning to visitors is blunt: if you are coming from the airport and later flying on to Hawaii, you are going to have a bag or two in the car, so avoid the most obvious touristy places, where your car is likely to get broken into. Thieves specifically target out-of-state license plates and rental cars — they know the trunk contains luggage, laptops, and cameras. The break-in takes under 60 seconds. Visitors have watched multiple cars get broken into at Alamo Square in a single afternoon, most of them with out-of-state plates and presumably rentals.

The neighborhood around Fisherman's Wharf and the parking lot near the Golden Gate Bridge viewpoint are among the worst in the country for this crime. Police response is notoriously slow; one victim spent six hours at four different police stations trying to report a serious crime and still got no help. Your insurance claim will go through, but the vacation photos and sentimental items are gone forever.
scams.avoidance: Do not leave anything in the car — not in the trunk, not under a jacket, not in the glove box. Use public transit, Uber, or Waymo to get around San Francisco; renting a car is actively inadvisable. If you must drive, use paid garages inside buildings rather than surface lots near attractions. Remove all items from the car each time you park, even for a 5-minute stop. Consider renting a sedan rather than an SUV — the cargo area is less visible to break-in scouts.
scams.location: Fisherman's Wharf, Golden Gate Bridge parking lots, Lombard Street, Alamo Square, Chinatown periphery

scams.name: Fake Buddhist Monk Bracelet Hustle
scams.tldr: He presses a laminated card into your hands — it speaks of peace, meditation, and blessings.
scams.description:
He presses a laminated card into your hands — it speaks of peace, meditation, and blessings. Then he points to a clipboard full of names with dollar amounts next to them: $20, $50, $100. He stares at you expectantly. The bracelet is already on your wrist.

This is the fake monk scam, and San Francisco has battled it for years. The phenomenon has been covered repeatedly in the local and national press, with headlines warning that the fake monks are back and aggressively begging; SFGate, The New York Times, and KRON4 have all reported on the same operation.

The monks are not monks. They are typically workers from mainland China operating in organized teams, using the visual shorthand of religious dress to bypass the defensive instincts tourists would otherwise have. The bracelet-on-wrist technique is the same manipulation mechanic as the Las Vegas CD hustle: once you are physically holding the item, the social pressure to "donate" becomes crushing. Those who refuse often find the monk turning hostile, following them, or making a scene in public.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets and decline any object being pressed on you. Simply keep walking — it's not rude to ignore someone approaching you for money. If a bracelet is placed on your wrist, hand it back and walk away immediately. Real monks don't solicit donations from tourists on street corners. Don't make eye contact — it's the first step in the engagement.
scams.location: Fisherman's Wharf, Union Square, Ferry Building Embarcadero area

scams.name: Cable Car Pickpocket Crews
scams.tldr: You've waited 40 minutes in line at the Powell Street turnaround and you're finally on the cable car, jammed shoulder to shoulder with other tourists, cameras out, faces lit with excitement.
scams.description:
You've waited 40 minutes in line at the Powell Street turnaround and you're finally on the cable car, jammed shoulder to shoulder with other tourists, cameras out, faces lit with excitement. It's the perfect moment — and professional pickpockets know it. While you're leaning out for a photo of Nob Hill dropping away beneath you, someone is working your jacket pocket with practiced, surgical calm.

Travelers single out one line in particular: the F-Line streetcar along Market Street is famous for pickpocketing, probably because it is geared toward tourists. The cable cars and the F-Line streetcar are tourist magnets, and where tourists go in dense, distracted crowds, pickpocket teams follow.

The operations are often teams of two or three: one person creates a distraction — dropping something, asking a question, bumping into you — while another works your bag or pocket. This is standard operating procedure for the European-style tourist pickpocket rings that operate globally; the technique is the same in Paris, Rome, and on San Francisco's cable car lines.
scams.avoidance: Wear a front-facing fanny pack or keep valuables in a front pants pocket. Use a crossbody bag with a zipper that faces your body, not the crowd. Leave expensive cameras and extra cash at the hotel for cable car rides. Be especially alert during any 'accidental' physical contact in crowds. Board at less crowded stops rather than the chaotic Powell Street turnaround.
scams.location: Powell Street cable car turnaround, F-Line streetcar on Market Street

scams.name: Homeless Distraction / Aggressive Panhandling Near ATMs
scams.tldr: You insert your card, shield the keypad, and start the transaction — and then someone is suddenly right next to you, talking rapidly, asking for change, getting in your space.
scams.description:
You insert your card, shield the keypad, and start the transaction — and then someone is suddenly right next to you, talking rapidly, asking for change, getting in your space. Your card is out of the machine by the time you finally look up. Did they see your PIN? Did someone swap your card? You're not sure, and that uncertainty is exactly the point.

San Francisco's Tenderloin and Civic Center areas have a density of people experiencing homelessness that can be overwhelming to first-time visitors. Most are not criminals: homeless people in San Francisco are not all the same, and unless someone is panhandling, they are unlikely to try to talk to tourists. But a small number do use aggressive panhandling as cover for distraction theft.

The reality is stark. San Francisco has become deeply unsafe for locals and tourists alike in certain pockets, with open-air drug use everywhere and what amounts to an open fentanyl bazaar. The issue isn't hypothetical — the proximity of distressed individuals and the general chaos around certain transit hubs creates real opportunities for opportunistic theft.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks, hotels, or grocery stores rather than standalone sidewalk machines. Complete your ATM transaction, secure your cash, and walk purposefully before stopping. Don't display cash or valuable items while walking through the Tenderloin. Acknowledge panhandlers briefly and keep walking — engagement prolongs the interaction. Use contactless payment methods such as Apple Pay or Google Pay to avoid cash withdrawals entirely.
scams.location: Tenderloin district, Civic Center, Union Square edges, near BART entrances

scams.name: Fake Charity Clipboard Solicitation
scams.tldr: You're window shopping on Union Square when a person with a clipboard and a vest reading "Save the Children" steps directly into your path.
scams.description:
You're window shopping on Union Square when a person with a clipboard and a vest reading "Save the Children" steps directly into your path. "Can you sign our petition?" You stop. They hand you the clipboard and a pen. As you read through it, they're talking fast, filling the silence, asking how you feel about the cause. By the time you've signed, they're asking for a credit card number for a "small monthly donation."

These operations use the social capital of legitimate charities to extract financial commitments on the street. While not always technically illegal, they are considered manipulative by consumer protection groups. Some use names nearly identical to those of real charities; others are entirely fabricated. The tactics are high-pressure and designed to make refusal feel like a moral failing.

San Francisco's heavy foot traffic and progressive-leaning tourist demographic make it a particularly effective operating ground. As one local put it, tourists have been getting robbed since before they were even called tourists, and the city shares its government's inability to handle economic inequality. The scam often moves in seasons, clusters near busy shopping areas, and uses young workers who may not even realize they are part of a problematic organization.
scams.avoidance: If you want to donate to a cause, look it up on Charity Navigator when you're home. Never provide financial information to anyone soliciting on the street. A polite 'sorry, I'm in a hurry' and keeping your stride is all you need. Legitimate charities don't need a street signature to help their cause. If you do sign a petition, you are under no obligation to donate afterward.
scams.location: Union Square, Fisherman's Wharf, near Ferry Building, Market Street

scams.name: Overpriced Sourdough and Clam Chowder Tourist Traps
scams.tldr: The restaurant seating you down at Fisherman's Wharf, with laminated menus and a line out the door, is absolutely charging you $35 for a bowl of clam chowder in a sourdough bread bowl that a local would get elsewhere for $12.
scams.description:
The restaurant seating you down at Fisherman's Wharf, with laminated menus and a line out the door, is absolutely charging you $35 for a bowl of clam chowder in a sourdough bread bowl that a local would get elsewhere for $12. The prices are printed right there on the menu. You're the one who sat down.

Locals have catalogued this category relentlessly. The practical advice is consistent: San Francisco is best explored on foot, so avoid renting a car, because parking is difficult in the dense areas of the city. And the implicit warning running through visitor accounts never changes — Pier 39 and the Fisherman's Wharf restaurant row are for the photo, not the food.

The 'scam' is the manufactured aura of authenticity. These restaurants have perfected the visual cues of a classic San Francisco seafood shack while charging luxury prices and serving tourist-grade food. The crab stands, the sourdough bread shop queues, and the famous clam chowder bowls are all engineered tourist traps. By all means add a day or two to your time in San Francisco — it is a beautiful city with plenty to see — just eat where locals eat.
scams.avoidance: Walk two blocks away from the waterfront and prices drop dramatically. Search Yelp for 'clam chowder SF locals recommend' rather than tourist-facing hits. The Boudin Bakery on the wharf is overpriced — buy sourdough at any Safeway for the real thing. Avoid restaurants with outdoor hosts or laminated picture menus. Ask your hotel concierge where local office workers eat lunch near the waterfront.
scams.location: Fisherman's Wharf restaurants, Pier 39, tourist-facing stalls on the Embarcadero
